title: Cello
summary: Cello notes played through a computed cello body. Limits first: A3 and the low notes are too dark, several notes are too clean, and the stopped notes sit off pitch. Every note drives a computed spruce and maple shell body with an air cavity, a finite-width hair bow, the measured rosin friction law of Woodhouse and Galluzzo (2025, eq. 13) and the printed 116 mm after-length. E2 sits 5.0 c flat of equal temperament and E3 8.1 c flat, each after one finger move and one residual-flexibility row and with its bow moved to 1/11 of its sounding length, and F5 holds a line at a third of its pitch. Eb4 is rendered at 47944 Hz to remove time-step lines and plays with the body's wood loss raised 3.25 times, near the printed damping, which takes away most of its too-clean fault but holds a cluster of lines near 180 Hz about 10 dB over the recording's. D3 and A3 keep 512 body modes, the others 256.
physics_present: a computed cello shell body from published plate geometry and wood data: spruce top, maple back and ribs, a 12.5 mm-class table, a 19 g bridge and 256 computed modes (D3 and A3 keep 512; D3's last mode is about 4.3 kHz)

an enclosed air cavity through a physical neck, and f-holes placed from printed caliper measurements of the Castelbarco Stradivari (Library of Congress); the C2 page's physics list does not name the f-holes
the measured Kaplan string rows (Mansour 2016): tension, mass, bending stiffness and loss factors for the string played, with the bridge and bow flexibility

the exact static residual flexibility of each string's omitted bending modes (`residual-flexibility exact-static-green`): the row adds the string's omitted modes as one static compliance at the bridge and at a finger, with no fitted number; A3, C2, D3 and G2 carry it with its bow counterpart, E2 and E3 carry the support row alone (it takes the E3 note 4.5 c flat and its 180 Hz line down 11.6 dB, and the E2 note 4.8 c sharp), and Eb4 and F5 carry neither
a bow of finite width (a 10 mm ribbon) with hair compliance, driven by a gesture schedule of ramp, hold and lift; on D3 and A3 the bow force follows the bow speed through the start of the stroke

on E3 and E2 the bow sits 1/11 of the sounding length from the bridge, as on the open pages (25.1 mm of 276.6 mm and 50.1 mm of 551.0 mm), with the force from Schelleng's limits at that distance (the maximum goes as v/beta and the minimum as v/beta^2: Mansour, Woodhouse and Scavone 2017, eqs 3-5; the force is the geometric mean of the window: E3 1.47 N in 0.47 to 4.60 N, E2 1.50 N in 0.49 to 4.60 N); F5 and Eb4 keep the open string's 62.7 mm bow distance, which is 0.285 and 0.129 of their sounding lengths
the measured rosin friction curve (Woodhouse and Galluzzo 2025, eq. 13) on every note
the printed 116 mm after-length, bridge to tailpiece (Fouilhe and Houssay, SMAC 2013), on every note

stopped notes: a rigid finger stop on the fingerboard (Issanchou 2017) at 1e12 N/m on the C string (E2, E3) and 1e13 N/m on the A string (F5, and Eb4 as its page), placed at the equal-tempered station and then moved once toward the named note, never toward the recording, on E2, E3 and F5; Eb4's finger is not moved
Eb4 rendered at 47944 Hz, a rate chosen so its period is a whole number of samples, and resampled to 48 kHz for the page

Eb4 plays with the body's wood loss raised 3.25 times; on free decay that takes the shell's lower strong pole from Q 67-75 with wood alone to Q 24-27, read on F5 and C2 renders with the same packs, near the 18-26 printed for a cello on a rig (Zhang and Woodhouse 2014); every other cello page keeps the wood-only loss
physics_missing: a measured cello: the body is computed from published geometry and wood data, and no measured body admittance or string Q of this instrument is on the cards; on the C2 page the wood data are stated only from 150 Hz (maple) and 100 Hz (spruce), so that body has no mode below 150 Hz, above the C2 fundamental
body modes above the computed range: 256 modes end at 2438.5 Hz (the 512 modes of D3 and A3 at about 4.3 kHz, read for D3); the plates are resolved to about 3 kHz and the ribs not above about 1 kHz

body damping: the shell's lowest strong pole reads Q 72-78 from wood alone (free decay 67-75, receiver sweep 78), against 18 to 26 printed for a cello on a rig or foam and 13.4 held by a player (Zhang and Woodhouse 2014); the F5 page names this as a likely reason for its fault, not shown. The wood loss raised 3.25 times toward the printed damping was tried on all eight cello pages: one rose (Eb4, 10 to 11 of 14) and it darkened every page, bringing the three too-bright pages toward their recordings and the five too-dark ones away. So more wood loss isn't what the cello's top end is missing
a body-radiation skin row: the posted cards carry none

a bow that varies during the note: force and speed hold after the ramp (D3's and A3's force follows speed only through the start), so the notes repeat too exactly: harmonics-to-noise reads 43.4 dB against 30.1 in the recording on E2 and 37.4 against 30.1 on C2 (Eb4, with the printed wood loss, reads 34.9 against 37.9); the Eb4 attack is far too quick, 37 ms against 411

time-step independence: at 48 kHz a note's period can lock to the render clock and put lines into the sound that are not in the instrument; Eb4 needed its own render rate, and F5 still holds a line at exactly a third of its pitch (233.0 Hz, -28.8 dB)

an explanation of the finger: the bowed pitch moves 1.4 to 1.8 times the length of the move (E3 25.3 c for 17.6 c before its residual row, which takes a further 4.5 c off the note, E2 19.2 c for 10.7 c before its row, which takes a further 4.8 c up), so E2 and E3 land flat of equal temperament, and the E3 and F5 recordings sit sharp of it

the bow's omitted-mode compliance on a stopped note: the engine refuses `bow-residual-flexibility` with a finger stop (the bow/stop cross-compliance is not yet carried), so E2 and E3 have the support row only and Eb4 and F5 have neither row; F5 was tried with the support row and fell from 9 to 8 of 15 (harmonics-to-noise left its ruler, the third harmonic rose to 23.7 dB re the first, and a held line appeared at 189 Hz, -19 dB), so it stays without

the timbre balance: the low notes and A3 are too dark (centroid 245 Hz against 388 on C2, 181 against 390 on E2, 249 against 575 on E3, 295 against 868 on A3) and F5 too bright (1936 against 1187; Eb4, with the printed wood loss, is 455 against 466); D3's first two harmonics are swapped (H2 7.7 dB over H1, the recording 7.5 dB under); on F5 the third harmonic leads with the first 15.7 dB under it, the recording the other way

the stopped notes' bow: F5 and Eb4 are not yet at 1/11 of their sounding lengths, and each needs its force from the limits (the A string's 0.7071 N is not checked against them); E3 at 1/11 and the page's 0.4204 N broke to its octave (0.90 times Schelleng's minimum, rendered 11-04). With the bow at 1/11 the E3 holes at H4 and H5 did not close (-0.8 and +2.7 dB re the first), which sit in a valley of the shell's bridge mobility at 818-870 Hz; E2 now builds in level by 5.7 dB over the note, its second harmonic no longer leads its first (-2.8 dB re the first against +5.5 in the recording), and it carries a burst near the body's 190 Hz mode at 0.8-1.6 s, which no grader row measures

lines that are not harmonics: C2 shows two about 18 dB over the recording (163.9 and 174.8 Hz), untraced; Eb4 holds a cluster at 165-195 Hz, -36 dB re its first harmonic against the recording's -46, strongest at 178.6 Hz, which no grader row measures
the other strings: only the bowed string is on a card, so there is no sympathetic ringing and no string-to-string coupling through the body
the rosin's temperature-dependent behaviour, transfer layer and contact history: eq. 13 is a velocity law measured at steady sliding
